---
title: "Non-correlations"
format: html
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

batting_raw <- read_csv("data/batting.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Season = as.character(Season))

batting <- batting_raw |>
  filter(PA >= 50)

set.seed(42)
```

This page uses static snapshots of the same D1 Softball batting data as the Explorer. Each plot shows player-seasons with at least 50 plate appearances; Pearson's _r_ summarizes the direction and strength of a linear association.

## Batting average and strikeouts

Unlike OBP and SLG, strikeouts have little linear association with batting average in these data (Pearson's _r_ = **-0.16**). Strikeouts are one way an at-bat can end, but batting average depends on hits divided by at-bats; players can have similar batting averages while having different numbers of at-bats and strikeouts. The slight trend should not be read as a strong relationship.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(batting, aes(BA, K)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1f4e79", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Batting Average (BA)", y = "Strikeouts (K)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Batting average and walks

Walks also have only a weak association with batting average (Pearson's _r_ = **0.31**). A walk is not counted as an at-bat, so it does not directly raise or lower batting average. Differences in plate appearances and player roles can still make the counts vary, which is why the points are spread out rather than forming a strong trend.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(batting, aes(BA, BB)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1f4e79", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Batting Average (BA)", y = "Walks (BB)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
